newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: YACHTING-BT GLOBAL CHALLENGE LEADER SAILS INTO NZ.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-BT GLOBAL CHALLENGE LEADER SAILS INTO NZ.

text.p: The leading yacht in the BT Global Challenge race sailed into Wellington Harbour on Monday to be greeted by a cannon, bagpipes and hundreds of spectators.
Group 4 was the first of the 14 yachts to reach its destination in the second leg of the epic race, after 40 days' sailing from Rio de Janeiro.

Organisers said celebrations would proceed over the next five days despite an overnight tragedy in Wellington Harbour, where four people died and one was missing after a fishing boat and a container ship collided.

More than 500 onlookers greeted the yacht, which made agonisingly slow progress in the final stages because of abnormally calm conditions -- in contrast to the weather further north where the tail end of former tropical cyclone Fergus was lashing north-eastern coasts.
A New Zealander on board Group 4, Grant Winfield, said he made the mistake of warning his crewmates about Wellington's notoriously windy weather.

"They asked me about windy Wellington and I said: 'Yes, it gets pretty windy there,' and all of a sudden we came round the corner and that was it, it (the wind) died," Winfield told a group of journalists.
"Fifteen hours later we're still sitting there going 'Oh, no' and I was getting grief about it," he said.
The boat finally drifted across the finish line seven miles ahead of nearest rival, Save the Children, which had cut her lead by about 40 miles.
"In the last hour we could see 'Save the Kids' in the distance, so there was definitely huge relief when we crossed the line," Winfield said.
"It was a great trip. We didn't have too much rough weather, and generally we had about 25-30 knots. It did quiet down every now and then but we had up to 45 knots ... it was a good crossing."

Winfield declined to predict whether Group 4 would win the race, which is billed as the world's toughest because vessels are sailing the "wrong way" around the globe, against prevailing winds and currents.
"I'd like to win it, obviously -- it would be very nice. We've won two legs now, but there are still four legs to go and it's still anybody's race."
